label: lem:grading
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:grading}
Choose a basis $u_1,\ldots,u_{2n}$ of $\mathfrak L$ and the basis
$w^1,\ldots,w^{2n}$ of $\overline\mathfrak L$ determined by
$2\langle u_a,w^b\rangle=\delta_a^b$.
For $0\ne\rho\in K$, the vectors
\[
s_I=c(w^{i_1})\cdots c(w^{i_r})\rho,
\qquad I=\{i_1<\cdots<i_r\}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,2n\},
\]
with $s_\varnothing=\rho$, form a basis of $S$, and $K=\mathbb C\rho$.
Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:grading}
\mathfrak U^{n-r}=\bigwedge^r\overline\mathfrak L\cdot K
\qquad(0\le r\le2n).
\end{equation}
Then
\[
S=\bigoplus_{j=-n}^n\mathfrak U^j,\qquad
\dim\mathfrak U^j=\binom{2n}{n-j},\qquad
\overline{\mathfrak U^j}=\mathfrak U^{-j},
\]
and Clifford multiplication satisfies
\[
c(\mathfrak L)\mathfrak U^j\subseteq\mathfrak U^{j+1},\qquad
c(\overline\mathfrak L)\mathfrak U^j\subseteq\mathfrak U^{j-1}.
\]
Moreover, there are natural vector-space isomorphisms
\begin{equation}\label{eq:spinor-cochain-map}
\begin{aligned}
F_r:\mathfrak U^{n-r}&\longrightarrow C^r(\mathfrak L,K)
=\bigwedge^r\mathfrak L^*\otimes K,\\
F_r(\alpha)(v_1,\ldots,v_r)&=c(v_r)\cdots c(v_1)\alpha.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
We set $\mathfrak U^j=0$ outside $-n\le j\le n$ and extend $F_r$ by zero
outside $0\le r\le2n$.
head: environment

label: eq:contraction
title: Proof
body_md:
Put $a_a=c(u_a)$ and $b_a=c(w^a)$. Isotropy and the Clifford
relation imply
\[
a_aa_b+a_ba_a=b_ab_b+b_bb_a=0,
\qquad a_ab_b+b_ba_a=\delta_a^b\operatorname{id}_S.
\]
Moving $a_a$ through a monomial and using $a_a\rho=0$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:contraction}
a_as_I=
\begin{cases}
0,&a\notin I,\\
(-1)^{t-1}s_{I\setminus\{a\}},&a=i_t.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
Suppose a linear relation among the $s_I$ has a nonzero coefficient
indexed by a set $I=\{i_1<\cdots<i_r\}$ of maximal size.
Applying $a_{i_r}\cdots a_{i_1}$ kills every other term with a
nonzero coefficient and sends $s_I$ to $\rho$, a contradiction.
The $2^{2n}$ monomials therefore form a basis of $S$.
For fixed $a$, distinct monomials containing $a$ are sent by $a_a$
to distinct basis vectors, up to sign. A vector annihilated by all
$a_a$ can consequently have only its $s_\varnothing$ coefficient
nonzero. This proves $K=\mathbb C\rho$.
Grouping monomials by their length proves the direct decomposition,
the dimensions, and the two grading shifts.

Conjugation can also be read directly from this basis. The nonzero
top monomial $s_{\rm top}=b_1\cdots b_{2n}\rho$ is annihilated by
all $b_a$. Conjugating the definition of $K$ identifies this common
annihilator with $\overline K=\mathbb C\bar\rho$, so $s_{\rm top}$ spans it.
Repeated use of~\eqref{eq:contraction} shows that
$\bigwedge^r\mathfrak L\cdot s_{\rm top}$ is spanned by all $s_I$ of
length $2n-r$. Hence
\[
\overline{\mathfrak U^{n-r}}
=\bigwedge^r\mathfrak L\cdot\overline K
=\mathfrak U^{r-n}.
\]

Finally, the values of $F_r$ lie in $\mathfrak U^n=K$ by the grading shifts,
and the map is alternating because Clifford operators from $\mathfrak L$
anticommute. For $w_1,\ldots,w_r\in\overline\mathfrak L$, the relations give
\[
F_r\bigl(c(w_1)\cdots c(w_r)\rho\bigr)(v_1,\ldots,v_r)
=\det\bigl(2\langle v_i,w_j\rangle\bigr)\rho.
\]
This identifies the monomial basis with the usual alternating
cochain basis and proves the last assertion.

label: prop:integrable-differentials
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:integrable-differentials}
If $\mathcal J$ is integrable, then $\delta_+=\delta_-=0$. Consequently,
\[
\mathrm d=\partial+\overline\partial,\qquad
\partial^2=\overline\partial^2=0,\qquad
\partial\overline\partial+\overline\partial\partial=0.
\]
Moreover, a non-degenerate pure spinor $\rho$ defines an integrable
structure if and only if $\mathrm d\rho=c(z)\rho$ for some $z\in \overline{\mathfrak{L}}$.
head: environment

label: eq:integrable_delta=0
title: Proof
body_md:
The shift $-3$ in~\eqref{eq:dcubic} comes from the Clifford products of three
    factors $\xi^a,\xi^b,[X_a,X_b] \in \overline\mathfrak L$ in the expression~(\ref{eq:dec_dif_Clifact}). Let $\alpha \in \mathfrak{U}^{j}$, the degree $-3$ part in $\mathrm d \alpha$ is $c(v)c(u)c(w) \mathrm d \alpha$ for $v,u,w \in \mathfrak{L}$, disregarding some non-zero scalar. The operator identities just proved imply
    \[
    \begin{aligned}\label{eq:integrable_delta=0}
    c(w)c(v)c(u)\mathrm d\alpha
    &=c(w)c(v)D_u\alpha\\
    &=c(w)\bigl(D_uc(v)-c([\![ u,v]\!])\bigr)\alpha\\
    &=-c(w)c([\![ u,v]\!])\alpha
    =-2\langle[\![ u,v]\!],w\rangle\alpha.
    \end{aligned}
    \]
    If $\mathfrak L$ is involutive, this tensor vanishes by isotropy. Hence
    $\delta_-=0$ on all of $S$. The reality of $\mathrm d$ and the conjugation statement in Lemma~\ref{lem:grading} give $\delta_+=0$ as well.
    Now the components of $\mathrm d^2$ with shifts $2,0,-2$ vanish separately,
    giving the three asserted differential identities.

    The relation~\ref{eq:integrable_delta=0} holds for $\alpha = \rho \in \mathfrak{U}^{n}$. For integrable $\mathcal J$, the equality
    $\mathrm d\rho=\overline\partial\rho\in\mathfrak U^{n-1}=c(\overline\mathfrak L)\rho$
    provides $z$. Conversely, if $\mathrm d\rho=c(z)\rho$, its triple
    contraction by elements of $\mathfrak L$ is zero. The preceding calculation
    then gives $\langle[\![ u,v]\!],w\rangle=0$ for all $u,v,w\in\mathfrak L$.
    Maximal isotropy implies $[\![ \mathfrak L,\mathfrak L]\!]\subseteq\mathfrak L$, proving
    integrability.
head: environment

label: prop:canonical-complex
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:canonical-complex}
With the action $v\cdot s=D_vs$ on $K$, the maps
$F_p$ of~\eqref{eq:spinor-cochain-map} make the following diagram commute
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=large]
\cdots \arrow[r] & \mathfrak{U}^{n-p+1} \arrow[r, "\overline{\partial}"] \arrow[d, "F_{p-1}"] & \mathfrak{U}^{n-p} \arrow[r, "\overline{\partial}"] \arrow[d, "F_{p}"] & \mathfrak{U}^{n-p-1} \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "F_{p+1}"] & \cdots \\
\cdots \arrow[r] & C^{p-1}(\mathfrak L,K)  \arrow[r, "\mathrm d_{\mathfrak L,K}"] & C^{p}(\mathfrak L,K) \arrow[r, "\mathrm d_{\mathfrak L,K}"] & C^{p+1}(\mathfrak L,K) \arrow[r] & \cdots
\end{tikzcd}
\]
in other words,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:chain-identification}
F_{p+1}\overline\partial=\mathrm d_{\mathfrak L,K}F_p.
\end{equation}
After choosing $\rho$ to identify $K$ with $\mathbb C_\chi$, the differential
on the right is $\mathrm d_{\mathfrak L,\chi}=\mathrm d_\mathfrak L+\chi\wedge$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Take $\alpha\in\mathfrak U^{n-p}$ and $v_0,\ldots,v_p\in\mathfrak L$, and
write $c_i=c(v_i)$ and $D_i=D_{v_i}$.
The grading gives
$c_p\cdots c_0\alpha=c_p\cdots c_0\partial\alpha=0$.
Therefore
\[
F_{p+1}(\overline\partial\alpha)(v_0,\ldots,v_p)
=c_p\cdots c_0\mathrm d\alpha.
\]
Successively substitute $c_i\mathrm d=D_i-\mathrm d c_i$ to obtain
\[
c_p\cdots c_0\mathrm d\alpha
=\sum_{i=0}^p(-1)^i
c_p\cdots c_{i+1}D_i c_{i-1}\cdots c_0\alpha;
\]
the last term, $(-1)^{p+1}\mathrm d(c_p\cdots c_0\alpha)$, is zero.
Move $D_i$ to the far left using
$c_jD_i=D_ic_j-c([\![ v_i,v_j]\!])$ for $j>i$.
The term in which $D_i$ reaches the left acts on a value of $F_p$
in $K$, so it gives the $i$th coefficient-action term of
\eqref{eq:CE}. A bracket contribution for $i<j$ initially has
sign $(-1)^{i+1}$. To place that bracket in the first cochain
argument, move its Clifford factor to the far right, across
$j-1$ other factors. Because all these factors belong to the
isotropic space $\mathfrak L$, each interchange contributes only a minus
sign. The resulting sign is $(-1)^{i+j}$.
Writing $\widetilde\alpha=F_p(\alpha)$, we obtain
\begin{align*}
F_{p+1}(\overline\partial\alpha)(v_0,\ldots,v_p)
&=\sum_{i=0}^p(-1)^i v_i\cdot
\widetilde\alpha(v_0,\ldots,\widehat v_i,\ldots,v_p)\\
&\quad+\sum_{i<j}(-1)^{i+j}
\widetilde\alpha([\![ v_i,v_j]\!],v_0,\ldots,
\widehat v_i,\ldots,\widehat v_j,\ldots,v_p).
\end{align*}
This is the coefficient differential~\eqref{eq:CE}, proving
\eqref{eq:chain-identification}.
head: environment

label: eq:ACK
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first isomorphism in cohomology follows from the isomorphism between the complexes in the proposition above. Since $\mathrm d$ is real and conjugation reverses the grading, it exchanges $\partial$ and $\overline\partial$. Conjugating the construction gives the second isomorphism in~\eqref{eq:ACK}.

    For the character formula, $c(v)\rho=0$ and the Clifford relation give
    \[
    \chi(v)\rho=c(v)c(z)\rho
    =2\langle v,z\rangle\rho-c(z)c(v)\rho
    =2\langle v,z\rangle\rho.
    \]
    This value is independent of the choice of $z$: any two choices
    differ by an element of the Clifford annihilator $\operatorname{Ann}(\rho)=\{u\in E:c(u)\rho=0\}=\mathfrak L$, which pairs trivially
    with $\mathfrak L$.
    Finally, $F_1(\mathrm d\rho)=\chi\otimes\rho$, and $F_1$ is an
    isomorphism. Thus $\chi=0$ is equivalent to $\mathrm d\rho=0$.

label: thm:L-almost-abelian
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{thm:L-almost-abelian}
Let $\mathcal J$ be an invariant generalized complex structure on
$\mathfrak g_A$, with eigenspace $\mathfrak L$ and canonical character $\chi$. Then
the map
\[
\phi:\mathfrak L\longrightarrow\mathbb C,\qquad \phi(X+\xi)=e^0(X),
\]
is a surjective Lie algebra homomorphism with abelian kernel
$\mathfrak n$. Hence, for any $Z\in\mathfrak L$ with $\phi(Z)=1$,
\[
\mathfrak L=\mathbb C Z\ltimes_C\mathfrak n,\qquad
C=\operatorname{ad}_Z|_{\mathfrak n}:\mathfrak n\to\mathfrak n,\qquad
\dim_\mathbb C\mathfrak n=2n-1.
\]
The endomorphism $C$ does not depend on the choice of $Z$.
Moreover, $\chi|_{\mathfrak n}=0$. Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:chi-phi}
\chi=\tau\phi,\qquad \tau=\chi(Z),
\end{equation}
and $\tau$ does not depend on the choice of $Z$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The vector part of $[\![ u,v]\!]$ lies in $[\mathfrak g_A,\mathfrak g_A]\subseteq\mathfrak h_\mathbb C$
by~\eqref{eq:cotangent-bracket}. Hence $\phi([\![ u,v]\!])=0$, and $\phi$ is a
homomorphism to the abelian Lie algebra $\mathbb C$. If $\phi=0$, the vector
projections of both $\mathfrak L$ and $\overline\mathfrak L$ would lie in $\mathfrak h_\mathbb C$. This
contradicts $E=\mathfrak L\oplus\overline\mathfrak L$. Thus $\phi$ is surjective, and
$\mathfrak n=\ker\phi$ is an ideal of dimension $2n-1$.

Take $X+\xi,\,Y+\eta\in\mathfrak n$, so that $X,Y\in\mathfrak h_\mathbb C$. Then
$[X,Y]=0$. For $W\in\mathfrak h$ the convention
$(\operatorname{ad}_X^*\eta)(W)=-\eta([X,W])$ gives zero, while for $W=e_0$ it gives
$\eta(AX)$. Therefore
\[
[\![ X+\xi,Y+\eta]\!]=\bigl(\eta(AX)-\xi(AY)\bigr)e^0 .
\]
By integrability, this element lies in $\mathfrak L$. Its pairing with $Z$ is
$\tfrac12\bigl(\eta(AX)-\xi(AY)\bigr)\phi(Z)$. Isotropy of $\mathfrak L$ forces
this pairing, and hence the bracket, to vanish. Thus $\mathfrak n$ is
abelian, and the semidirect-product decomposition follows. If
$\phi(Z')=1$, then $Z'-Z\in\mathfrak n$. Hence
$\operatorname{ad}_{Z'}|_{\mathfrak n}=\operatorname{ad}_Z|_{\mathfrak n}$.

For the character, fix $0\ne\rho\in K$. By~\eqref{eq:dgA} we can write
$\mathrm d\rho=e^0\wedge\beta$ for some $\beta\in S$. Let
$v=X+\xi\in\mathfrak n$, so that $e^0(X)=0$. Then
\[
c(v)(e^0\wedge\beta)
=\iota_X(e^0\wedge\beta)+\xi\wedge e^0\wedge\beta
=-e^0\wedge c(v)\beta .
\]
By~\eqref{eq:character}, $\chi(v)\rho=c(v)\mathrm d\rho\in e^0\wedge S$.
Suppose $\chi(v)\ne0$. Then $\rho\in e^0\wedge S$, so
$c(e^0)\rho=e^0\wedge\rho=0$, and $e^0\in\operatorname{Ann}(\rho)=\mathfrak L$. Since $e^0$ is
real, it would also lie in $\overline\mathfrak L$. This is impossible because
$\mathfrak L\cap\overline\mathfrak L=0$. Hence $\chi|_{\mathfrak n}=0$. The linear forms
$\chi$ and $\chi(Z)\phi$ agree on $Z$ and on $\mathfrak n$, which
gives~\eqref{eq:chi-phi}. Finally, $\chi(Z')=\chi(Z)$ whenever
$Z'-Z\in\mathfrak n$.
head: environment

label: def:PsiC
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:PsiC}
Let $\Psi_C$ be the degree-zero derivation of $\bigwedge^\bullet\mathfrak L^*$
determined by
\[
\Psi_C(1)=0,\qquad
\Psi_C\xi=\xi\circ\operatorname{ad}_Z\quad(\xi\in\mathfrak L^*).
\]
With the coadjoint convention of~\eqref{eq:cotangent-bracket}, this
means $\Psi_C\xi=-\operatorname{ad}_Z^*\xi$ on $\mathfrak L^*$.
head: environment

label: eq:almost-d
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Both sides are degree-one derivations of $\bigwedge^\bullet\mathfrak L^*$.
For the right-hand side, this holds because $\Psi_C$ is a degree-zero
derivation and $\phi$ has degree one. It is therefore enough to compare
the two sides on scalars and on $\mathfrak L^*=\mathbb C\phi\oplus\mathfrak n^*$.
Both vanish on scalars. By~\eqref{eq:CE-trivial},
$(\mathrm d_\mathfrak L\phi)(u,v)=-\phi([\![ u,v]\!])=0$, and also $\Psi_C\phi=0$.

Let $\eta\in\mathfrak n^*$. Since $\mathfrak n$ is abelian,
$(\mathrm d_\mathfrak L\eta)(y,y')=0$ for $y,y'\in\mathfrak n$. Moreover,
$(\mathrm d_\mathfrak L\eta)(Z,y)=-\eta(Cy)$. The two-form $-\phi\wedge\Psi_C\eta$
takes the same values, because $\Psi_C\eta$ vanishes on $Z$ and
restricts to $\eta\circ C$ on $\mathfrak n$. The value of a two-form
on $Z$ and $\mathfrak n$ determines it, which proves~\eqref{eq:almost-d}.
head: environment

label: lem:wang
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:wang}
Let $\mathcal J$ be an invariant generalized complex structure on
$\mathfrak g_A$, and let $\tau$ be as in~\eqref{eq:chi-phi}. Put
\[
\Psi_p=\Psi_C|_{\bigwedge^p\mathfrak n^*}-\tau\operatorname{id}
\qquad(0\le p\le 2n-1),
\]
and let $\Psi_p$ be the zero map of the zero space otherwise.
Then, for $0\le p\le 2n$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:wang}
GH_{\overline\partial}^{n-p}(\mathfrak g_A)\cong H^p(\mathfrak L,\mathbb C_\chi)
\cong\ker\Psi_p\oplus\operatorname{coker}\Psi_{p-1}.
\end{equation}
Let $c_1,\ldots,c_{2n-1}$ be the eigenvalues of $C$, with algebraic
multiplicity. The eigenvalues of $\Psi_p$ are then
$\sum_{i\in I}c_i-\tau$, where $I$ runs over index subsets of size $p$.
If $C$ is diagonalizable, so is $\Psi_p$, and $\dim\ker\Psi_p$ is the
number of these sums that vanish.
head: environment

label: eq:two-term
title: Proof
body_md:
The first isomorphism is~\eqref{eq:ACK}. By~\eqref{eq:cochain-splitting},
a $p$-cochain can be written uniquely as $\alpha+\phi\wedge\beta$, with
$\alpha\in\bigwedge^p\mathfrak n^*$ and
$\beta\in\bigwedge^{p-1}\mathfrak n^*$. We use~\eqref{eq:twist},
\eqref{eq:chi-phi} and~\eqref{eq:almost-d}, together with $\mathrm d_\mathfrak L\phi=0$
and $\phi\wedge\phi=0$. They give
$\mathrm d_\mathfrak L(\phi\wedge\beta)=-\phi\wedge\mathrm d_\mathfrak L\beta=0$, and hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:two-term}
\mathrm d_{\mathfrak L,\chi}(\alpha+\phi\wedge\beta)
=-\phi\wedge\Psi_C\alpha+\tau\phi\wedge\alpha
=-\phi\wedge\Psi_p\alpha.
\end{equation}
The complex is therefore the direct sum, over $p$, of the two-term
complexes
\[
\bigwedge^p\mathfrak n^*
\xrightarrow{\;-\phi\wedge\Psi_p\;}
\phi\wedge\bigwedge^p\mathfrak n^*,
\]
placed in degrees $p$ and $p+1$. The map $\phi\wedge$ is injective on
$\bigwedge^\bullet\mathfrak n^*$. Hence the summand indexed by $p$
contributes $\ker\Psi_p$ in degree $p$, and the summand indexed by $p-1$
contributes $\operatorname{coker}\Psi_{p-1}$ in degree $p$. This proves~\eqref{eq:wang}. The isomorphism sends $(\alpha,[\beta])$ to the class of
$F_p^{-1}\bigl((\alpha+\phi\wedge\beta)\otimes\rho\bigr)$.

For the spectrum, triangularize $C^T$ on $\mathfrak n^*$
and use~\eqref{eq:Psi-expanded}. The operator $\Psi_C$ then acts
triangularly on wedge monomials, with diagonal entries $\sum_{i\in I}c_i$.
Subtracting $\tau$ proves the spectral assertion. When $C$ is
diagonalizable, an eigenbasis of $C^T$ gives a wedge eigenbasis of
$\Psi_p$, which proves the kernel count.

title: Theorem

name: *{Theorem A

label: lem:model-integrability
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $Ae_j=a_je_j$. By~\eqref{eq:dgA}, $\mathrm d e^0=0$ and
$\mathrm d e^j=-a_je^0\wedge e^j$ for $j\ge1$. Hence
\[
\mathrm d\omega_s=0,\quad \mathrm d(e^0\wedge e^d)=0,\quad
\mathrm d\theta_i=-\lambda_i e^0\wedge\theta_i,
\quad
\mathrm d(e^0+\mathbf i e^d)=-\mu e^0\wedge(e^0+\mathbf i e^d).
\]
For instance,
$\mathrm d(e^{r}\wedge e^{r+1})=-\zeta e^0\wedge e^r\wedge e^{r+1}
+\zeta e^0\wedge e^r\wedge e^{r+1}=0$ when $a_r=-a_{r+1}=\zeta$.
Moving $e^0$ to the front of $\Theta$ produces signs that cancel those
of the Leibniz rule, so $\mathrm d\Theta=-\bigl(\sum_i\lambda_i\bigr)e^0\wedge\Theta$.
The graded Leibniz rule then proves~\eqref{eq:Lambda}.

For non-degeneracy, the normal-form condition reads
$\omega^{n-k}\wedge\Omega\wedge\overline\Omega\ne0$. In Model~I,
$n-k=s+1$ and $\omega^{s+1}=(s+1)\,e^0\wedge e^d\wedge\omega_s^s$.
In Model~II, $n-k=s$, and
$(e^0+\mathbf i e^d)\wedge(e^0-\mathbf i e^d)=-2\mathbf i e^0\wedge e^d$. In both cases,
the product is therefore a nonzero multiple of
\[
e^0\wedge e^d\wedge\omega_s^s\wedge\Theta\wedge\overline\Theta,
\]
which is a volume form. Since $\mathrm d\rho=c(-\Lambda e^0)\rho$,
Proposition~\ref{prop:integrable-differentials} proves integrability.
head: environment

label: prop:specC
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:specC}
For either spinor in~\eqref{eq:models}, let $\mathfrak L=\operatorname{Ann}(\rho)$, and let
$\phi,\mathfrak n,C$ be as in Proposition~\ref{thm:L-almost-abelian},
with $Z$ given by the table below. Then $C$ is diagonalizable and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C-spectrum}
\Sigma:=\operatorname{spec}(C)
=\{\pm\lambda_1,\ldots,\pm\lambda_h,
\pm\zeta_1,\ldots,\pm\zeta_s,\nu\},
\end{equation}
where
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
\text{model}&\text{type}& Z&\nu&\Lambda\\\hline
\mathrm I&h&e_0-\mathbf i e^d&\mu&\sum_i\lambda_i\\
\mathrm {II}&h+1&e_0+\mathbf i e_d&-\mu&\mu+\sum_i\lambda_i
\end{array}
\]
The canonical character is $\chi=-\Lambda\phi$; that is, $\tau=-\Lambda$.
If $\mathfrak g_A$ is unimodular, then $\operatorname{tr} C=-2\Lambda$.
head: environment

label: eq:annihilator
title: Proof
body_md:
For a two-form $\gamma$, the Clifford action~\eqref{eq:clifford}
satisfies
\[
c(X+\xi-\iota_X\gamma)(e^\gamma\wedge\alpha)
=e^\gamma\wedge c(X+\xi)\alpha,
\]
because $\iota_X(e^\gamma\wedge\alpha)
=\iota_X\gamma\wedge e^\gamma\wedge\alpha+e^\gamma\wedge\iota_X\alpha$.
If $\Omega$ is decomposable, the two components of
$c(X+\xi)\Omega$ have different degrees. Consequently, for
$\rho=e^{\mathbf i\omega}\wedge\Omega$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:annihilator}
\operatorname{Ann}(\rho)=\{X-\mathbf i\iota_X\omega+\xi:
\iota_X\Omega=0,\ \xi\wedge\Omega=0\}.
\end{equation}
The vectors $Z$ in the table satisfy these conditions and have
$\phi(Z)=1$. In both models, define
\[
v_i=e_{2i}-\mathbf i e_{2i-1},\qquad
p_m=e_{r_m}-\mathbf i e^{r_m+1},\qquad
q_m=e_{r_m+1}+\mathbf i e^{r_m}.
\]
A basis of $\mathfrak n$ consists of $\theta_i,v_i$ ($1\le i\le h$) and
$p_m,q_m$ ($1\le m\le s$), together with the additional element
\[
w_{\mathrm I}=e_d+\mathbf i e^0,\qquad
w_{\mathrm {II}}=e^0+\mathbf i e^d.
\]
Indeed, each of these elements satisfies~\eqref{eq:annihilator} and has
$\phi=0$. Their vector parts span the solutions $X$ of the vector
conditions with $e^0(X)=0$; this space has dimension $h+2s+1$ in
Model~I and $h+2s$ in Model~II. The remaining pure covectors span the
solutions $\xi$ of $\xi\wedge\Omega=0$, of dimension $h$ and $h+1$,
respectively. Altogether there are $2h+2s+1=2n-1$ independent elements.

By~\eqref{eq:cotangent-bracket}, the coadjoint terms are
\[
\operatorname{ad}_{e_0}^*|_{\mathfrak h^*}=-A^T,\qquad
\operatorname{ad}_{e_0}^*e^0=0,\qquad
\operatorname{ad}_Y^*\eta=\eta(AY)e^0\quad(Y\in\mathfrak h_\mathbb C).
\]
In both models these formulas give
\[
[\![ Z,\theta_i]\!]=-\lambda_i\theta_i,\quad
[\![ Z,v_i]\!]=\lambda_i v_i,\quad
[\![ Z,p_m]\!]=\zeta_m p_m,\quad
[\![ Z,q_m]\!]=-\zeta_m q_m.
\]
The possible extra terms $\eta(AY)e^0$ vanish here, since
$e^d(AY)=0$ for $Y=v_i,e_{r_m},e_{r_m+1}$, and $\eta(Ae_d)=\mu\,\eta(e_d)=0$ for $\eta=\theta_i,e^{r_m},e^{r_m+1}$. For the exceptional
elements,
\[
[\![ e_0-\mathbf i e^d,e_d+\mathbf i e^0]\!]
=\mu e_d+\mathbf i\mu e^0=\mu w_{\mathrm I},
\]
and
\[
[\![ e_0+\mathbf i e_d,e^0+\mathbf i e^d]\!]
=-\mathbf i\mu e^d-\mu e^0=-\mu w_{\mathrm {II}}.
\]
Thus the displayed basis is an eigenbasis for $C$.

By~\eqref{eq:Lambda} we may take $z=-\Lambda e^0$ in~\eqref{eq:chi}.
This gives $\chi(X+\xi)=2\langle-\Lambda e^0,X+\xi\rangle
=-\Lambda e^0(X)$, so $\chi=-\Lambda\phi$, in accordance
with~\eqref{eq:chi-phi}. Finally, unimodularity means
$0=\operatorname{tr} A=2\sum_i\lambda_i+\mu$, and $\operatorname{tr} C=\nu$. This gives
$\mu=-2\Lambda_{\mathrm I}$ and $-\mu=-2\Lambda_{\mathrm {II}}$, proving
the trace assertion.
head: environment

label: thm:master
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:master}
For either structure~\eqref{eq:models}, list the indexed spectrum of $C$
as $c_1,\ldots,c_{2n-1}$, and set
\[
N_p=\#\left\{I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,2n-1\}:|I|=p,
\ \sum_{i\in I}c_i=-\Lambda\right\}\quad(0\le p\le 2n-1),
\]
with $N_p=0$ otherwise. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:master}
\dim GH_{\overline\partial}^{n-p}(\mathfrak g_A)=N_p+N_{p-1}\quad(0\le p\le2n).
\end{equation}
Equivalently, let
$P_\rho(t)=\sum_{p=0}^{2n}\dim GH_{\overline\partial}^{n-p}(\mathfrak g_A)\,t^p$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:genfun}
P_\rho(t)=(1+t)[q^{-\Lambda}]\prod_{i=1}^{2n-1}(1+tq^{c_i}).
\end{equation}
Here the product lies in the group algebra $\mathbb Z[\mathcal A][t]$, where
$\mathcal A\subset\mathbb R$ is the additive group generated by
$c_1,\ldots,c_{2n-1},\Lambda$. The symbols satisfy
$q^\gamma q^{\gamma'}=q^{\gamma+\gamma'}$, and the bracket denotes
coefficient extraction. If $\operatorname{tr} A=0$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:symmetry}
N_p=N_{2n-1-p},\qquad
\dim GH_{\overline\partial}^j(\mathfrak g_A)=\dim GH_{\overline\partial}^{-j}(\mathfrak g_A).
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition~\ref{prop:specC}, Lemma~\ref{lem:wang} applies with
$\tau=-\Lambda$ and diagonalizable $C$. For an eigenbasis $\eta_i$ of
$C^T$, one has
\[
\Psi_p(\eta_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge\eta_{i_p})
=\left(\sum_{a=1}^p c_{i_a}+\Lambda\right)
\eta_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge\eta_{i_p}.
\]
Thus $\dim\ker\Psi_p=N_p$. Since $\Psi_{p-1}$ is an endomorphism,
rank--nullity gives $\dim\operatorname{coker}\Psi_{p-1}=N_{p-1}$, and~\eqref{eq:wang}
proves~\eqref{eq:master}. Expanding the product in~\eqref{eq:genfun}
shows that its $q^{-\Lambda}$ coefficient is $\sum_pN_pt^p$.
Multiplication by $1+t$ gives $P_\rho$.

When $\operatorname{tr} A=0$, Proposition~\ref{prop:specC} gives
$\sum_i c_i=-2\Lambda$. A subset has sum $-\Lambda$ exactly when its
complement does, which proves $N_p=N_{2n-1-p}$. Substituting $2n-p$ for $p$
in~\eqref{eq:master} then gives
$\dim GH_{\overline\partial}^{p-n}=N_{p-1}+N_p=\dim GH_{\overline\partial}^{n-p}$.

label: cor:generic
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:generic}
Assume $\operatorname{tr} A=0$ and that the indexed family
$\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_h,\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_s$ is linearly
independent over $\mathbb Q$. For either model,
\[
N_{h+2r}=N_{h+2r+1}=\binom{s}{r}\quad(0\le r\le s),
\qquad N_p=0\text{ otherwise}.
\]
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:generic-polynomial}
P_\rho(t)=t^h(1+t)^2(1+t^2)^s,
\end{equation}
and
\[
\sum_j\dim GH_{\overline\partial}^j(\mathfrak g_A)=2^{s+2},\qquad
GH_{\overline\partial}^j(\mathfrak g_A)=0\quad\text{if }|j|>n-h.
\]
To express this in terms of the type $k$, substitute $(h,s)=(k,n-k-1)$
for Model~I and $(h,s)=(k-1,n-k)$ for Model~II.

label: ex:generic
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:generic}
Suppose $\lambda,\kappa$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$ and
$\operatorname{spec}(A)=\{\lambda,-\lambda,\kappa,\kappa,-2\kappa\}$.
For Model~II with $h=s=1$, $\lambda_1=\kappa$, $\zeta_1=\lambda$ and
$\mu=-2\kappa$, the type is $2$. Moreover, $\Lambda=-\kappa$ and
$\Sigma=\{\lambda,-\lambda,\kappa,-\kappa,2\kappa\}$.
By Corollary~\ref{cor:generic},
\[
P_\rho(t)=t(1+t)^2(1+t^2),\qquad
(\dim GH_{\overline\partial}^{3},\ldots,\dim GH_{\overline\partial}^{-3})=(0,1,2,2,2,1,0).
\]

label: lem:averaging
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $X_1,\ldots,X_{2n}$ be the invariant frame dual to
$\xi^1,\ldots,\xi^{2n}$. Then
\[
\mathrm d(f\xi^I)=\sum_aX_a(f)\,\xi^a\wedge\xi^I+f\,\mathrm d\xi^I,
\]
and $\mathrm d\xi^I$ is invariant. By unimodularity,
$\mathcal L_{X_a}\mathrm{vol}_X=-\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}_{X_a})\mathrm{vol}_X=0$, so
Stokes' theorem gives
\[
\int_XX_a(f)\,\mathrm{vol}_X
=\int_X\mathrm d\iota_{X_a}(f\,\mathrm{vol}_X)=0 .
\]
Hence
$\operatorname{Av}\mathrm d(f\xi^I)=\bigl(\int_Xf\,\mathrm{vol}_X\bigr)\mathrm d\xi^I
=\mathrm d\operatorname{Av}(f\xi^I)$.
By~\eqref{eq:invariant-frame},
$\operatorname{Av}(f\alpha)=\bigl(\int_Xf\,\mathrm{vol}_X\bigr)\alpha$
for $\alpha\in\mathfrak U^j$. Thus $\operatorname{Av}$ maps $U^j(X)$ onto
$\mathfrak U^j$ and commutes with the projections $\operatorname{pr}_j$. By
\eqref{eq:projected-differentials}, it commutes with $\partial$ and
$\overline\partial$. Since $\operatorname{Av}$ is a projection onto $\mathfrak U^\bullet$, the
decomposition follows. The last assertion follows from the reality of
$\operatorname{Av}$ and $\overline{U^j(X)}=U^{-j}(X)$.

label: prop:reduction-to-dbar
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:reduction-to-dbar}
For each of $GH_{\overline\partial}$, $GH_\partial$, $GH_{BC}$ and $GH_A$, the
inclusion of invariant forms induces an injection
$GH^j(\mathfrak g_A)\hookrightarrow GH^j(X)$. Its cokernel is the corresponding
cohomology of $Q^\bullet$ in degree $j$. If $H_{\overline\partial}(Q^\bullet)=0$, all
four injections are isomorphisms.
head: environment
name: *{Corollary 5.2

label: prop:bundle-construction
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:bundle-construction}
Suppose $\mathfrak h=\mathfrak h_c\oplus\mathfrak k$ is a sum of $A$-invariant subspaces
with $\dim\mathfrak h_c=2k-1$, $\dim\mathfrak k=2\ell$ and $k+\ell=n$ (so
$k\ge1$). Then $\mathfrak k$ is an abelian ideal of $\mathfrak g_A$, and
$\mathfrak b=\mathfrak g_A/\mathfrak k$ is the almost abelian Lie algebra
$\mathfrak g_{A_c}$ with $A_c=A|_{\mathfrak h_c}$. Assume that $\mathfrak b$ carries an
integrable complex structure $J_B$, with
$\mathfrak b_\mathbb C=\mathfrak b^{1,0}\oplus\mathfrak b^{0,1}$, and that a
closed real two-form $\omega$ on $\mathfrak g_A$ restricts to a symplectic form
$\sigma$ on $\mathfrak k$. Let $\pi:\mathfrak g_A\to\mathfrak b$ be the quotient
map, let $0\ne\Omega\in\bigwedge^k\mathfrak b^{*1,0}$, and write
$\mathrm d_{\mathfrak b}\Omega=\alpha_B\wedge\Omega$ with
$\alpha_B\in\mathfrak b^{*0,1}$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bundle-spinor}
\rho=e^{\mathbf i\omega}\wedge\pi^*\Omega
\end{equation}
defines an invariant generalized complex structure of type $k$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bundle-character}
\mathrm d\rho=c(\pi^*\alpha_B)\rho,\qquad
\chi(X+\xi)=\alpha_B(\pi X)\quad(X+\xi\in\mathfrak L).
\end{equation}
Moreover, $A|_{\mathfrak k}\in\mathfrak{sp}(\mathfrak k,\sigma)$.
head: environment
name: *{Theorem C

label: lem:L-extension
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:L-extension}
In the setting of Proposition~\ref{prop:bundle-construction}, regard
$J_B$ as a generalized complex structure on $\mathfrak b$. Its eigenspace
and canonical line are
\[
\mathfrak L_B=\mathfrak b^{0,1}\oplus\mathfrak b^{*1,0},\qquad
K_{\mathfrak b}=\bigwedge^k\mathfrak b^{*1,0}=\mathbb C\Omega,
\]
and by~\eqref{eq:chi} its canonical character is
$\chi_B(Y+\vartheta)=\alpha_B(Y)$. Put
\[
\mathcal B(X+\xi)=X+\xi-\mathbf i\iota_X\omega,\qquad
\mathfrak S=\mathcal B(\mathfrak k_\mathbb C)
=\{u-\mathbf i\iota_u\omega:u\in\mathfrak k_\mathbb C\}.
\]
Then the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathcal B$ is an automorphism of the Lie algebra
$\left(E=(\mathfrak g\oplus\mathfrak g^*)_\mathbb C,[\![ \cdot,\cdot]\!]\right)$, and $\mathfrak L=\mathcal B(\mathfrak L_0)$, where
\[
\mathfrak L_0=\{X+\pi^*\vartheta:\ \pi X\in\mathfrak b^{0,1},\
\vartheta\in\mathfrak b^{*1,0}\}.
\]
\item The map $\varpi:\mathfrak L\to\mathfrak L_B$ given by
$\varpi\bigl(\mathcal B(X+\pi^*\vartheta)\bigr)=\pi X+\vartheta$ is a
surjective Lie algebra homomorphism with kernel $\mathfrak S$. The ideal
$\mathfrak S$ is abelian and is contained in the ideal $\mathfrak n$ of
Proposition~\ref{thm:L-almost-abelian}.
\item $\chi=\chi_B\circ\varpi$, and $\Omega\mapsto
e^{\mathbf i\omega}\wedge\pi^*\Omega$ is an isomorphism of $\mathfrak L$-modules
$\varpi^*K_{\mathfrak b}\cong K$.
\item For $u\in\mathfrak k_\mathbb C$, $\vartheta\in\mathfrak b^{*1,0}$, and
$\widetilde Y\in\mathfrak g_{A,\mathbb C}$ with $\pi\widetilde Y\in\mathfrak b^{0,1}$,
\[
[\![ \mathcal B\widetilde Y,\mathcal Bu]\!]
=e^0(\widetilde Y)\,\mathcal B(Au),\qquad
[\![ \mathcal B\pi^*\vartheta,\mathcal Bu]\!]=0 .
\]
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The identity used in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:specC}, applied
to the closed two-form $\mathbf i\omega$, gives
$c(\mathcal Bv)(e^{\mathbf i\omega}\wedge\beta)=e^{\mathbf i\omega}\wedge c(v)\beta$
for every form $\beta$. Since $\mathrm d\omega=0$, the operator
$e^{\mathbf i\omega}\wedge$ commutes with $\mathrm d$. By~\eqref{eq:Cartan-operator},
conjugation by $e^{\mathbf i\omega}\wedge$ sends $D_u$ to $D_{\mathcal Bu}$,
and~\eqref{eq:D-identities} gives
$c([\![ \mathcal Bu,\mathcal Bv]\!])=c(\mathcal B[\![ u,v]\!])$. As $c$ is
injective on $E$, $\mathcal B$ preserves the bracket. The same identity
gives $\mathfrak L=\operatorname{Ann}(\rho)=\mathcal B\bigl(\operatorname{Ann}(\pi^*\Omega)\bigr)$. The two
components of $c(X+\xi)\pi^*\Omega$ have different degrees. Hence $X+\xi$
annihilates $\pi^*\Omega$ exactly when $\iota_{\pi X}\Omega=0$ and
$\xi\wedge\pi^*\Omega=0$, that is, when $\pi X\in\mathfrak b^{0,1}$ and
$\xi\in\pi^*\mathfrak b^{*1,0}$. This proves the first part.

Since $\pi$ is a homomorphism,
$(\operatorname{ad}_X^*\pi^*\vartheta)(W)=-\vartheta([\pi X,\pi W])$, that is,
$\operatorname{ad}_X^*\pi^*\vartheta=\pi^*\operatorname{ad}_{\pi X}^*\vartheta$.
By~\eqref{eq:cotangent-bracket}, the map
$X+\pi^*\vartheta\mapsto\pi X+\vartheta$ is therefore a homomorphism
$\mathfrak L_0\to\mathfrak L_B$. It is surjective, and its kernel is $\mathfrak k_\mathbb C$
because $\pi^*$ is injective. Composing with $\mathcal B^{-1}$ gives
$\varpi$. The ideal $\mathfrak S$ is abelian because $\mathfrak k_\mathbb C$ is.
Since $\mathcal B$ does not change vector parts,
$\phi(\mathcal Bu)=e^0(u)=0$ for $u\in\mathfrak k_\mathbb C$, so
$\mathfrak S\subseteq\mathfrak n$.

For $v=X+\pi^*\vartheta\in\mathfrak L_0$ we have
$c(v)\pi^*=\pi^*c(\pi X+\vartheta)$ and $\mathrm d\pi^*=\pi^*\mathrm d_{\mathfrak b}$,
hence $D_v\pi^*=\pi^*D_{\varpi\mathcal Bv}$. Together with the first
part,
\[
D_{\mathcal Bv}(e^{\mathbf i\omega}\wedge\pi^*\Omega)
=e^{\mathbf i\omega}\wedge\pi^*\bigl(D_{\varpi\mathcal Bv}\Omega\bigr)
=\chi_B(\varpi\mathcal Bv)\,e^{\mathbf i\omega}\wedge\pi^*\Omega .
\]
By~\eqref{eq:character}, this proves the third part.

Finally, $u\in\mathfrak h_\mathbb C$ and $[\mathfrak h,\mathfrak h]=0$ give
$[\![ \widetilde Y,u]\!]=[\widetilde Y,u]=e^0(\widetilde Y)Au$.
By~\eqref{eq:cotangent-bracket} and the formula above,
$[\![ \pi^*\vartheta,u]\!]=-\operatorname{ad}_u^*\pi^*\vartheta
=-\pi^*\operatorname{ad}^*_{\pi u}\vartheta=0$. Applying the automorphism $\mathcal B$
proves the last part.
head: environment

label: lem:GM
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:GM}
Extend $\eta\in V^q$ to $\mathfrak g_{A,\mathbb C}$ by zero on $\mathbb R e_0\oplus\mathfrak h_c$. The
resulting invariant form restricts to a closed form on each fiber of
$p$, and its fiberwise class $s_\eta$ is a smooth section of
$\mathcal H^q$. As $\eta$ runs over a basis of $V^q$, these sections
form a frame. For $Y\in\mathfrak b_\mathbb C$ and its invariant vector field
$Y^L$ on $B$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:GM-frame}
\nabla_{Y^L}(fs_\eta)=Y^L(f)\,s_\eta+f\,s_{Y\cdot\eta}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, $\eta\mapsto s_\eta$ induces an isomorphism of holomorphic
bundles $\mathcal V^q\cong(\mathcal H^q,\nabla^{0,1})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The fiber through $\Gamma g$ is the image of $gG_{\mathfrak k}$, and
the extended form restricts there to an invariant form on a torus. Such
forms are closed and represent each cohomology class exactly once. This
proves the first two assertions. The Gauss--Manin derivative
$\nabla_Y[\tilde s]$ is represented by the fiberwise restriction of
$\mathcal L_{\widetilde Y}\tilde s$, for any lift $\widetilde Y$ of $Y$.
Take the invariant vector field of a lift $\widetilde Y\in\mathfrak g_{A,\mathbb C}$.
On invariant arguments $u_j\in\mathfrak k_\mathbb C$, the invariant form
$\mathcal L_{\widetilde Y}\eta$ takes the value given
by~\eqref{eq:fiber-action}. The Leibniz rule gives~\eqref{eq:GM-frame}.
Taking $Y\in\mathfrak b^{0,1}$ and comparing with $\overline\partial_{\mathcal V^q}$
proves the last assertion.
head: environment

label: prop:spectral-sequences
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:L-extension},
$\mathfrak S$ is an abelian ideal of $\mathfrak L$ and
$\chi|_{\mathfrak S}=\chi_B\circ\varpi|_{\mathfrak S}=0$. The
filtration~\eqref{eq:filtration} is the Hochschild--Serre filtration of
the ideal $\mathfrak S$. The resulting spectral sequence has
\[
\widetilde E_1^{p,q}
=H^q\bigl(\mathfrak S,\textstyle\bigwedge^p\mathfrak L_B^*\otimes K\bigr),
\qquad
\widetilde E_2^{p,q}=H^p\bigl(\mathfrak L_B,H^q(\mathfrak S,K)\bigr).
\]
Since $\mathfrak S$ is abelian and acts trivially on $K$ and on
$\mathfrak L/\mathfrak S$, the differentials of its cochain complexes vanish.
Hence $H^q(\mathfrak S,K)=\bigwedge^q\mathfrak S^*\otimes K$. The map
$\mathcal B$ identifies $\bigwedge^q\mathfrak S^*$ with $V^q$, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:L-extension} identifies the induced $\mathfrak L_B$-action
with~\eqref{eq:fiber-action}, where $\mathfrak b^{*1,0}$ acts trivially.
The same lemma identifies $K$ with $\varpi^*K_{\mathfrak b}$. This
gives~\eqref{eq:invariant-SS}, and~\eqref{eq:ACK} identifies the
abutment.

The form $\omega$ is closed on $X$, so
$\mathcal B$ is an automorphism of the complexified Courant bracket on
sections \cite{Gualtieri2011}. Pointwise, the first part of
Lemma~\ref{lem:L-extension} gives $L_X=\mathcal B(L_{0,X})$, where
\[
L_{0,X}=\{Y+\xi:\ p_*Y\in T^{0,1}B,\ \xi\in p^*T^{*1,0}B\}.
\]
The vertical bundle $T(X/B)_\mathbb C\subset L_{0,X}$ is a subalgebroid.
Projectable sections of $L_{0, X}$ induce the anchor and bracket of $L_B$.
Hence $S_X$ is a subalgebroid of $L_X$ with $L_X/S_X\cong p^*L_B$, and
the differential preserves~\eqref{eq:filtration}. The graded pieces are
\[
\operatorname{gr}^pC^{p+q}
=\Gamma\bigl(X,\textstyle\bigwedge^qS_X^*\otimes
p^*(\bigwedge^pL_B^*\otimes K_B)\bigr)
\]
by~\eqref{eq:canonical-pullback}. The bracket of a vertical vector field
with a projectable section is vertical. By~\eqref{eq:canonical-pullback},
$S_X$ also annihilates the pulled-back frames of $K_X$. Thus $S_X$ acts
on the coefficients by the flat partial connection whose parallel sections
are pulled back from $B$, and $d_0$ is the vertical de Rham differential
with coefficients in $p^*(\bigwedge^pL_B^*\otimes K_B)$. As the fibers
are compact, fiberwise Hodge theory gives
\[
E_1^{p,q}=\Gamma\bigl(B,\textstyle\bigwedge^pL_B^*\otimes K_B
\otimes\mathcal H^q\bigr).
\]
The differential $d_1$ is induced by projectable lifts. Along a lift of
a section of $T^{0,1}B$, it differentiates fiberwise classes by the
Gauss--Manin connection. The lift $\mathcal B(p^*\vartheta)$ of a section
$\vartheta$ of $T^{*1,0}B$ has zero bracket with vertical sections and
acts trivially. Together with~\eqref{eq:canonical-pullback}, this
identifies $(E_1,d_1)$ with $C^\bullet(L_B,K_B\otimes\mathcal H^q)$ and
gives~\eqref{eq:global-SS}. The abutment is identified
by~\eqref{eq:global-ACK}. This is the spectral sequence
of~\cite{ACK}*{Theorem~2.1}, with coefficient bundle $p^*K_B$ and
ordinary vertical degree $q$.

 The elements of $\mathfrak S$ are invariant sections
spanning $S_X$ at every point. Hence invariant cochains in
$F^pC^m(\mathfrak L,K)$ span $F^pC^m(L_X,K_X)$ over $C^\infty(X)$, and the
inclusion of invariant cochains is filtered. On the first page, it is the
inclusion of invariant sections, with $\eta\in V^q$ sent to $s_\eta$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:GM}, it commutes with $d_1$.

 Let $M$ be a $\mathfrak b^{0,1}$-module,
regarded as an $\mathfrak L_B$-module on which $\mathfrak b^{*1,0}$ acts
trivially. By~\eqref{eq:cotangent-bracket}, $\mathfrak L_B$ is the semidirect
product of the subalgebra $\mathfrak b^{0,1}$ and the abelian ideal
$\mathfrak b^{*1,0}$, on which $\mathfrak b^{0,1}$ acts by the coadjoint
action. The ideal acts trivially on $K_{\mathfrak b}\otimes M$ because
$\chi_B$ vanishes on it. The differential~\eqref{eq:CE} therefore has no
terms coming from the action or the brackets of the ideal, and
\[
C^p(\mathfrak L_B,K_{\mathfrak b}\otimes M)
=\bigoplus_{r+b=p}C^b\bigl(\mathfrak b^{0,1},
\textstyle\bigwedge^r(\mathfrak b^{*1,0})^*\otimes K_{\mathfrak b}
\otimes M\bigr)
\]
as complexes. For $\bar Y\in\mathfrak b^{0,1}$ we have
$D_{\bar Y}\Omega=\iota_{\bar Y}\mathrm d\Omega=\mathcal L_{\bar Y}\Omega$.
Thus $K_{\mathfrak b}$ is the top exterior power of the coadjoint module
$\mathfrak b^{*1,0}$, and contraction is a $\mathfrak b^{0,1}$-equivariant
isomorphism
$\bigwedge^r(\mathfrak b^{*1,0})^*\otimes K_{\mathfrak b}\cong
\bigwedge^{k-r}\mathfrak b^{*1,0}$. With $a=k-r$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:canonical-to-Dolbeault}
H^p(\mathfrak L_B,K_{\mathfrak b}\otimes M)\cong
\bigoplus_{a-b=k-p}H^{a,b}_{\overline\partial}(\mathfrak b;M).
\end{equation}
The same argument with smooth sections uses the holomorphic isomorphism
$\bigwedge^rT^{1,0}B\otimes K_B\cong\Omega^{k-r}_B$. It identifies
$H^p(L_B,K_B\otimes\mathcal M)$ with
$\bigoplus_{a-b=k-p}H^b(B,\Omega^a_B\otimes\mathcal M)$, compatibly
with~\eqref{eq:comparison-map}. For $M=V^q$ and
$\mathcal M=\mathcal V^q\cong\mathcal H^q$, this
proves~\eqref{eq:second-pages} and the description of the morphism.

label: thm:invariance
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:invariance}
Assume that $\mathcal J$ is given by~\eqref{eq:bundle-spinor} and that
$\Gamma$ satisfies~\eqref{eq:lattice-hypotheses}. Suppose that the
comparison maps
\begin{equation}\label{eq:comparison-hypothesis}
H_{\overline\partial}^{a,b}(\mathfrak b;V^q)
\longrightarrow H^b(B,\Omega_B^a\otimes\mathcal H^q)
\end{equation}
are isomorphisms for all $0\le a,b\le k$ and $0\le q\le2\ell$. Then the
inclusion of invariant forms induces isomorphisms
\[
GH_{\overline\partial}^j(\mathfrak g_A)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }GH_{\overline\partial}^j(X)
\qquad\text{for all }j.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition~\ref{prop:spectral-sequences} and the hypothesis, the
inclusion $\widetilde E_2\to E_2$ is an isomorphism. By
\eqref{eq:SS-splitting}, $E_2(Q)=0$. The filtration is finite, with
$0\le p\le2k$ and $0\le q\le2\ell$, so $H_{\overline\partial}(Q)=0$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:reduction-to-dbar} completes the proof.
head: environment

label: cor:BC-invariance
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:BC-invariance}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:invariance}, invariant forms
also compute $GH_\partial^j(X)$, $GH_{BC}^j(X)$ and $GH_A^j(X)$ for
every $j$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:invariance} shows that $H_{\overline\partial}(Q)=0$.
Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:reduction-to-dbar}.

label: lem:characters
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:characters}
Let $\kappa_1,\ldots,\kappa_{2\ell}$ be the eigenvalues of
$A|_{\mathfrak k}$, listed with algebraic multiplicity, and put
$\kappa_I=\sum_{i\in I}\kappa_i$ for $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,2\ell\}$.
Then $V^q$ has a filtration by $\mathfrak b^{0,1}$-submodules whose
successive quotients are the modules $\mathbb C_{-\kappa_Ie^0}$ with $|I|=q$.
If $A|_{\mathfrak k}$ is diagonalizable, then
\[
V^q\cong\bigoplus_{|I|=q}\mathbb C_{-\kappa_Ie^0},\qquad
\mathcal H^q\cong\bigoplus_{|I|=q}\mathcal E_{\kappa_I}.
\]
Consequently,~\eqref{eq:comparison-hypothesis} holds provided that,
for all $0\le a,b\le k$ and every
$\kappa\in\{\kappa_I:I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,2\ell\}\}$, invariant forms
induce isomorphisms
\begin{equation}\label{eq:character-hypothesis}
H^{a,b}_{\overline\partial}(\mathfrak b;\mathbb C_{-\kappa e^0})
\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^b(B,\Omega^a_B\otimes\mathcal E_\kappa).
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Triangularize the transpose of $A|_{\mathfrak k}$ on
$\mathfrak k_\mathbb C^*$. As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:wang},
$\Psi_{\mathfrak k}$ is then triangular on wedge monomials, with
diagonal entries $\kappa_I$. Since $\mathfrak b^{0,1}$ acts by multiples
of $\Psi_{\mathfrak k}$, the corresponding flag of
$\Psi_{\mathfrak k}$-invariant subspaces is a flag of submodules with the
stated quotients. For diagonalizable $A|_{\mathfrak k}$, a wedge
eigenbasis splits it, and Lemma~\ref{lem:GM} transfers the splitting to
$\mathcal H^q$.

The construction $M\mapsto\mathcal M$ is exact. A short exact sequence of
modules gives short exact sequences of invariant and of smooth Dolbeault
complexes, compatible with the inclusion. By the resulting long exact
sequences and the five lemma, induction on the length of the flag shows
that~\eqref{eq:comparison-map} is an isomorphism for $M=V^q$ once it is
an isomorphism for the one-dimensional quotients.
head: environment

label: cor:modelII-quotients
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:modelII-quotients}
Let $A$ be diagonalizable over $\mathbb R$, let $\mathcal J$ be the Model~II structure
of~\eqref{eq:models}, and let $\mathfrak k$ and $\mathfrak b$ be as in
Section~\ref{subsec:adapted}. Assume that $\Gamma$
satisfies~\eqref{eq:lattice-hypotheses}, and
that~\eqref{eq:character-hypothesis} holds for every sum $\kappa$ of a
subfamily of $(\zeta_1,-\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_s,-\zeta_s)$. Then, with
$N_p$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:master},
\[
\dim GH^{n-p}_{\overline\partial}(X)=\dim GH^{p-n}_{\overline\partial}(X)=N_p+N_{p-1}
\qquad(0\le p\le2n),
\]
and invariant forms compute $GH_\partial$, $GH_{BC}$ and $GH_A$ of $X$.
Here $B$ is a compact quotient of $G_{\mathfrak b}$, whose Lie algebra
$\mathfrak g_{A_c}$ has
$\operatorname{spec}(A_c)=\{\lambda_1,\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_h,\lambda_h,\mu\}$ and
carries the Model~II complex structure.
head: environment

label: ex:lattice-dependence
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:lattice-dependence}
Let $n=2$, $h=0$ and $s=1$, with $\zeta=\zeta_1\ne0$. Since $\operatorname{tr} A=0$,
we have $\mu=0$. Thus $d=1$, $r_1=2$, and
\[
Ae_1=0,\qquad Ae_2=\zeta e_2,\qquad Ae_3=-\zeta e_3 .
\]
The Model~II spinor $\rho=e^{\mathbf i e^2\wedge e^3}\wedge(e^0+\mathbf i e^1)$ has
type $1$, with $\mathfrak k=\operatorname{span}\{e_2,e_3\}$. The algebra
$\mathfrak b$ is abelian, spanned by the images of $e_0$ and $e_1$. By
Corollary~\ref{cor:generic},
\[
\bigl(\dim GH^2_{\overline\partial},\ldots,\dim GH^{-2}_{\overline\partial}\bigr)(\mathfrak g_A)
=(1,2,2,2,1).
\]

Choose $M\in SL_2(\mathbb Z)$ with $\operatorname{tr} M\ge3$, and let $\lambda>1$ be its larger
eigenvalue. For $t_0=\log\lambda/|\zeta|$, the restriction of $e^{t_0A}$
to $\mathfrak k$ is conjugate to $M$. It therefore preserves a lattice
$\Gamma_{\mathfrak k}\subset\mathfrak k$. For $y_0>0$, put
\[
\Gamma=\mathbb Z t_0\ltimes\bigl(\mathbb Z y_0e_1\oplus\Gamma_{\mathfrak k}\bigr)<G_A .
\]
It satisfies~\eqref{eq:lattice-hypotheses} with
$\Gamma_{\mathfrak b}=\mathbb Z t_0\oplus\mathbb Z y_0$. The base $B$ is the elliptic
curve $\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z t_0+\mathbf i\mathbb Z y_0)$, with coordinate $z=x+\mathbf i y$, $e^0=\mathrm d x$
and $e^1=\mathrm d y$. The sums $\kappa_I$ lie in $\{0,\zeta,-\zeta\}$. Thus
$\mathcal H^0$ and $\mathcal H^2$ are holomorphically trivial, and
$\mathcal H^1\cong\mathcal E_\zeta\oplus\mathcal E_{-\zeta}$.

For $\kappa=0$,~\eqref{eq:character-hypothesis} holds, as on every
complex torus. For $\kappa=\pm\zeta$, the invariant side vanishes:
$\mathfrak b^{0,1}$ is spanned by $\bar w=\tfrac12(e_0+\mathbf i e_1)$, which
acts on $\bigwedge^a\mathfrak b^{*1,0}\otimes\mathbb C_{-\kappa e^0}$ by the
nonzero scalar $-\kappa/2$. On the other hand,
$(e^0)^{0,1}=\tfrac12\mathrm d\bar z$ and
$\overline\partial_Be^{\mathbf i\kappa y}=-\tfrac\kappa2e^{\mathbf i\kappa y}\mathrm d\bar z$. Hence
\[
\overline\partial_\kappa f=e^{-\mathbf i\kappa y}\,\overline\partial_B\bigl(\underbrace{e^{\mathbf i\kappa y}f}_{=:g}\bigr).
\]
For a function $f$ on $B$, the function $g=e^{\mathbf i\kappa y}f$ on $\mathbb C$
satisfies $g(z+t_0)=g(z)$ and $g(z+\mathbf i y_0)=e^{\mathbf i\kappa y_0}g(z)$. If
$g$ is holomorphic, $|g|$ is doubly periodic, so $g$ is constant, and it
vanishes unless $e^{\mathbf i\kappa y_0}=1$. Indeed,
\begin{align*}
    C=g(z+\mathbf i y_0)=e^{\mathbf i\kappa y_0}g(z)=e^{\mathbf i\kappa y_0}C\implies C(1-e^{\mathbf i \kappa y_0})=0.
\end{align*}
Thus $\mathcal E_\kappa$ is
holomorphically trivial if $\kappa y_0\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, with frame
$e^{-\mathbf i\kappa y}$. Otherwise, it is a nontrivial line bundle of degree
zero on an elliptic curve, and all its cohomology vanishes.

If $\zeta y_0\notin2\pi\mathbb Z$, Lemma~\ref{lem:characters} and
Theorem~\ref{thm:invariance} give $GH_{\overline\partial}(X)\cong GH_{\overline\partial}(\mathfrak g_A)$.
If $\zeta y_0\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, then~\eqref{eq:character-hypothesis} fails
for $\kappa=\pm\zeta$. In~\eqref{eq:SS-splitting}, $E_2(Q)$ vanishes in
the rows $q=0,2$ and equals the row $q=1$ of $E_2$. By
\eqref{eq:second-pages}, this row has dimensions $2,4,2$ for
$p=0,1,2$. A spectral sequence with a single nonzero row degenerates, so
\[
\bigl(\dim GH^2_{\overline\partial},\ldots,\dim GH^{-2}_{\overline\partial}\bigr)(X)
=(1,4,6,4,1).
\]
Thus, for the same $\mathfrak g_A$ and $\mathcal J$, invariant forms compute
$GH_{\overline\partial}(X)$ for some lattices but not for others. Notice that the dependence on the lattice is not a surprise; the Dolbeault cohomology of complex solvmanifolds is also known to vary with the choice of $\Gamma$, as in \cite{Kasuya13}*{Example 1}.
